## This tutorial

- This tutorial will revise/introduce some relevant R commands for this subject. 
- Introduce data on Retail sales for Australia that will be used for the first forecasting application in this subject.
  - Retail sales are considered a key indicator of the health of an economy, and are commonly a target of interest for commercial forecasters.
  
<blue>Before starting with the questions, let's warm up by setting up our workspace in RStudio. Usually the first step is to set up the **working directory**.</blue>


---

### Warming Up: Setting Up Working Directory in R

::: {.callout-note}
Setting up the <blue>working directory</blue> ensures that R can accurately locate where your data files are stored. It defines where R looks for files and where it saves outputs.
:::

To set up your working directory, enter command:
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

setwd("Your location goes here")
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
Alternatively, you can click on:
<blue>$$\boxed{\;\textsf{Session}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Set Working Directory}\;}\;\;\to\;\;\boxed{\;\textsf{Choose Directory}\;}$$</blue>


On my computer, it looks like:
<myimage src="figures/figure1.png" width="95%"></myimage>

## Question 1
::: {.callout-question}
Obtain the data file `RetailSales.csv`, and save it into an appropriate working directory. Read the data into an R dataframe. To get a sense of the variables in the dataframe, use the `head()` command to print out the first six rows of the dataframe. 
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

# Read data file and create monthly ts object
dt <- read.csv("RetailSales.csv")
print(head(dt))
```

## Question 2
::: {.callout-question}
We will focus on the time series of Total retail sales. Create a time series object for monthly total retail sales. Plot this time series.
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

Retail_m <- ts(dt$Total, frequency=12, start=c(1982,4), end=c(2024,9))
plot(Retail_m, main="Monthly Australian Retail Sales",
  ylab="Retail sales ($m)")
```

## Question 3(a) {.scrollable .shrink-output}
::: {.callout-question}
Use `aggregate` to transform the monthly time series to quarterly frequency. 
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

Retail_q <- aggregate(Retail_m, nfrequency=4)
```

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

❓ What's going on?

::: {.small-output}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

print(Retail_m)
```

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true

print(Retail_q)
```
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
::: {.callout-note}
`aggregate` generates a new series, `Retail_q`, by summing up the monthly observations of each quarter.
:::

## Question 3(b)
::: {.callout-question}
Create a window of this quarterly time series from 2000q1 to 2018q4, and produce a time series plot.
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
S_t <- window(Retail_q, start=c(2000,1), end=c(2018,4))
plot(S_t, main="Quarterly Australian Retail Sales",
  ylab="Retail sales ($m)")
```


## Question 4
::: {.callout-question}
Take the log of the quarterly time series and produce a plot.
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>
```{r}
Y_t <- log(S_t)
plot(Y_t, main="Retail sales (log), 2000q1 to 2018q4")
```

## Questions 5 and 6
::: {.callout-question}
Denote the log retail sales time series as $Y_{t}$. Create the *first difference* time series
$$\Delta Y_{t}=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}$$
Print out the first six values of $Y_{t}$ and $\Delta Y_{t}$. What’s going on with the value of 
$\Delta Y_{t}$ for 2000q1?
:::

<div style="height: 1em;"></div>
```{r}
# First difference of quarterly log retail sales Y_t, convert to pct
D_Y_t <- diff(Y_t)*100
print(round(head(cbind(Y_t,D_Y_t)),4))
```
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
::: {.callout-note}
The first value in `D_Y_t` is missing (`NA`) because there is no value of `Y_t` available before 10.3685 to compute the difference. Taking a difference of a time series will necessarily result in a shorter time series because of this.
:::

## Question 7
::: {.callout-question}
Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is
$$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$
Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 1em;"></div>
```{r}
# Percentage change of retail sales
R_t <- diff(S_t)/lag(S_t,-1)*100
# Compare
print(round(head(cbind(D_Y_t, R_t)),4))
```


## Question 7
::: {.callout-question}
Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series, that is
$$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%.$$
Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 1em;"></div>

What does `lag(S_t, -1)` function do?

```{r}
print(head(cbind(lag(S_t,-1),S_t)))
```

## Question 7 ctd: Why the comparison?

:::{.incremental}
- Adding 1 on both sides and take logs:
\begin{align}
R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\\
1+R_{t}&=\frac{S_{t}}{S_{t-1}}\\
\log(1+R_{t})&=\log(S_{t})-\log(S_{t-1})\\
\log(1+R_{t})&=Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}\equiv\Delta Y_{t}
\end{align}
- Then with the <blue>approximation $\log(1+R_{t})\approx R_{t}$</blue> for small values of $R_{t}$, we have $R_{t}\approx \Delta Y_{t}$:
$$\text{$R_{t}\approx\log(1+R_{t})$}= \Delta Y_{t}$$
:::

## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (1/2)
::: {.callout-question}
Denote the quarterly retail sales time series by $S_{t}$. Create a time series of the quarterly percentage change (growth rate) of this time series,
$R_{t}=\frac{S_{t}-S_{t-1}}{S_{t-1}}\times 100\%$.

Compare the values of $\Delta Y_{t}$ and $R_{t}$.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

::: {.callout-note}
The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes.
:::

<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>
For the entire time series the two variables are very highly correlated:
```{r}
print(cor(R_t, D_Y_t))
print(round(cor(R_t, D_Y_t), 3))
```


## Question 7 ctd: Some further observations (2/2)

::: {.callout-note}
The values of $\log S_{t}-\log S_{t-1}$ and $R_{t}=(S_{t}-S_{t-1})/S_{t-1}$ are quite similar especially for the smaller changes.
:::
<div style="height: 0.5em;"></div>

This is also evident in the plot shown below:
```{r}
plot(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(D_Y_t), pch=16, cex=0.7,
     xlab="Rt", ylab="DYt")
lines(as.numeric(R_t), as.numeric(R_t), col="blue")
```


## Question 7 ctd: Why taking logs differences?

- Taking log differences or simple returns is a common type of <blue>"filtering"</blue> in time series analysis.
- Filtering tends to stablise/linearise features such as trend and seasonality.
- Changes in a logged time series can be interpreted as approximately percentage changes, which is often convenient.
- Also, time series models, such as AR models and VAR models, requires data to be *stationary* <blue>$\to$ filtering/transformation ensures this requirement is met. </blue>
